final_proof:
Let \(v_p\) denote the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers, and put
\[
|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}\quad (x\ne0),\qquad |0|_p=0.
\]
The completion \(\mathbb Q_p\) of \(\mathbb Q\) under this absolute value satisfies the strong triangle inequality
\[
|x+y|_p\leq \max\{|x|_p,|y|_p\}.
\]

Let \(B=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N_0}\), where \(\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). For each binary sequence \(a=(a_0,a_1,\ldots)\in B\), define rational partial sums
\[
S_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_np^n.
\]
If \(M>N\) and \(S_M(a)-S_N(a)\ne0\), repeated use of the strong triangle inequality gives
\[
|S_M(a)-S_N(a)|_p
\leq \max_{\substack{N<n\leq M\\a_n\ne0}}|a_np^n|_p
\leq p^{-(N+1)}.
\]
The same bound is immediate when the difference is zero. Hence \((S_N(a))_N\) is Cauchy, so by completeness it has a limit in \(\mathbb Q_p\). Define
\[
\Phi(a)=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_np^n.
\]

We claim that \(\Phi\) is injective. Let \(a,b\in B\) be distinct, and let \(m\) be the least index for which \(a_m\ne b_m\). Then
\[
\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)=(a_m-b_m)p^m+R,
\qquad
R=\sum_{n=m+1}^{\infty}(a_n-b_n)p^n.
\]
The remainder series converges by the same Cauchy estimate, and its finite partial sums have absolute value at most \(p^{-(m+1)}\). Since the absolute value is continuous, it follows that
\[
|R|_p\leq p^{-(m+1)}.
\]
On the other hand, \(a_m-b_m\in\{1,-1\}\), and hence
\[
|(a_m-b_m)p^m|_p=p^{-m}>p^{-(m+1)}\geq |R|_p.
\]
For any non-Archimedean absolute value, \(|x|>|y|\) implies \(|x+y|=|x|\): the strong triangle inequality first gives \(|x+y|\leq|x|\), while applying it to \(x=(x+y)-y\) forces \(|x|\leq|x+y|\). Consequently,
\[
|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|_p=p^{-m}>0.
\]
Thus \(\Phi(a)\ne\Phi(b)\), proving that \(\Phi:B\to\mathbb Q_p\) is injective.

It remains to show that \(B\) is uncountable. If its elements could be listed as
\[
a^{(0)},a^{(1)},a^{(2)},\ldots,
\]
define \(c\in B\) by
\[
c_n=1-a^{(n)}_n.
\]
For every \(n\), the sequence \(c\) differs from \(a^{(n)}\) in coordinate \(n\), so \(c\) is absent from the alleged enumeration, a contradiction. Hence \(B\) is uncountable. Since the uncountable set \(B\) injects into \(\mathbb Q_p\), the set \(\mathbb Q_p\) is uncountable.
